extracted.intended_audience: USCIS adjudicators, DHS policymakers, immigration practitioners, and public commenters on the proposed public charge rule
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of whether an alien is likely to become a public charge under the DHS/USCIS proposed rule, using specified heavily weighed negative and positive factors and a totality-of-the-circumstances analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and skills as indicator of self-sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A person’s education and skills may be positive factors for purposes of evidencing self-sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS cites SIPP and Census Bureau data showing associations between higher educational attainment/skills and lower public benefit participation; education and skills are used as positive evidence in the totality of the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment / ability and prospect of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who is capable and able to work but does not work demonstrates a lack of self-sufficiency; conversely, full-time work is associated with lower likelihood of benefit receipt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS would consider current employment status and the reasonable prospect of future employment when weighing risk of becoming a public charge. Evidence of employment or strong prospect (e.g., pending job) is a positive indicator; long employment instability (cycling on/off benefits) is a negative indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Current receipt of one or more public benefits (heavily weighed negative factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Current receipt of one or more public benefits, as defined in proposed 8 CFR 212.21(b), would be a heavily weighed negative factor in a public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current receipt alone would not automatically justify a finding of inadmissibility, but it means the alien currently is a public charge under proposed 8 CFR 212.21(a) and suggests they may continue to receive benefits in the future. DHS cites program spell-length research (e.g., many participants stay 37–48 months) to support heavy weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past receipt of public benefits within 36 months (significant weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien’s past receipt of public benefits within the 36 months immediately preceding application carries significant weight in determining likelihood of becoming a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight depends on recency, whether benefits were received for extended periods (multiple years), at multiple time periods (e.g., multiple episodes in last two years), number of different benefits, and amounts received. Example: benefit received 5 years ago is a negative factor but less weight; one received 6 months before application would be a heavily weighed negative factor. DHS requests comment on appropriate lookback periods (e.g., 24-, 36-, or 48-month).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of benefit receipt: duration, frequency, multiplicity, and amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether benefits were received for an extended period (multiple years), at multiple different time periods, multiple different benefits, and the amounts received affect weight given to past receipt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS explicitly uses duration, frequency, multiplicity, and amounts to modulate the negative weight of past benefit receipt (e.g., long-term or repeated use and receipt of multiple benefits increases negative weight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial means to pay for medical costs (heavily weighed negative factor if absent)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien is at high risk of becoming a public charge if he or she does not have private health insurance or the financial resources to pay for reasonably foreseeable medical costs related to conditions likely to require extensive treatment or institutionalization or that will interfere with ability to provide self-care, attend school, or work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An alien may provide evidence of prospect of obtaining health insurance (e.g., pending employment with employer-sponsored insurance) to mitigate this negative factor. DHS cites evidence about high costs of chronic conditions to justify heavy weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical condition reported by panel physician or civil surgeon
rubrics_metrics.description: If a panel physician or civil surgeon reports a medical condition likely to require extensive medical treatment or institutionalization, or that will interfere with ability to provide for self, attend school, or work, this is a heavily weighed negative factor when the alien is uninsured, has public-benefit health coverage, or has no prospect of private health insurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS would rely on panel physician and civil surgeon examinations for determining whether the medical circumstance gives rise to the heavily weighted negative factor. The combination of costly/limiting medical condition plus lack of private means to pay is the trigger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alien previously found inadmissible or deportable based on public charge
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien previously found inadmissible or deportable based on public charge grounds is considered a high risk of becoming a public charge in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent countervailing positive factors and evidence showing current circumstances outweigh the conditions supporting the prior finding, the previous finding will carry heavy weight in determining likely future public-charge status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant income, assets, resources, or support as heavily weighed positive factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial assets, resources, support, or annual income of at least 250 percent of the Federal Poverty Guidelines (FPG) are proposed to be considered a heavily weighed positive factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS bases this on observed lower benefit participation rates as income increases. Income between 125 and 250 percent of FPG is considered a positive factor (but not as strongly). Having income/assets above thresholds does not automatically decide the case; all factors are considered in the totality of the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household member income and assets and other mitigating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Household members' income and assets, and other circumstances showing sufficient resources, may overcome negative factors related to lack of employment or benefit receipt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS would review household resources and other mitigating evidence in the totality of the circumstances to determine whether they overcome negative indicators of likely future benefit use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: All factors—negative and positive—are considered together in a totality of the circumstances determination of whether the alien is likely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single factor (except where specified as heavily weighed) automatically determines inadmissibility; adjudicators balance heavily weighed negative and positive factors (e.g., current/past benefits, health, income/assets, employment, education/skills, prior findings) to reach an overall judgment. DHS invites comment on elements such as appropriate lookback periods for past benefits.
